bib.title: AppAgent: Multimodal Agents as Smartphone Users

legacy_report:
SOURCE: AppAgent: Multimodal Agents as Smartphone Users. Chi Zhang, Zhao Yang, Jiaxuan Liu, Yucheng Han, Xin Chen, Zebiao Huang, Bin Fu, Gang Yu (Tencent). The file is arXiv:2312.13771v3 (stamped 5 Jul 2026), cs.CV. It carries no venue, so treat it as a preprint, 2023 (the note cites 2023).

COVERAGE: 42,091 of 42,091 chars read, 10 of 10 pages. Pages 1-8 are body text and page 9-10 are references. There are no appendices, and there is no human-study protocol section. I also read the target note, which already lists AppAgent in its GUI-agent table: "50 tasks across 10 apps".

CLAIMS (ranked)

- The simplified action space alone lifts GPT-4 from near-zero to about half of tasks.
  - number: SR 2.2% (raw) to 48.9% (simplified space). Reward 0.6 to 3.5. Avg steps 4.0 to 6.9.
  - setup: GPT-4 with no reference document, 45 tasks on 9 apps (Lightroom excluded). Success means finishing within 10 steps.
  - quote: "GPT4 (Baseline) None Raw 2.2% 0.6 4.0NoneOurs48.9% 3.5 6.9". The extraction of Table 1 is jumbled. The row reads GPT-4, no document, raw action space, then GPT-4, no document, "Ours" action space.
  - where: Table 1, p.7.

- A knowledge base from autonomous exploration raises success to 73.3%.
  - number: 73.3% SR, reward 5.1, 4.4 steps.
  - setup: same 45 tasks, 9 apps, GPT-4, "Auto. Exploration", simplified action space.
  - quote: "Auto. Exploration Ours73.3% 5.1 4.4"
  - where: Table 1, p.7.

- A knowledge base from watching human demonstrations reaches 84.4%.
  - number: 84.4% SR, reward 4.7, 5.1 steps.
  - quote: "Watching Demos Ours84.4% 4.7 5.1"
  - where: Table 1, p.7.

- A manually written document (the oracle) reaches 95.6%.
  - number: 95.6% SR, reward 5.5, 5.5 steps.
  - quote: "Manually Crafted Ours95.6% 5.5 5.5"
  - where: Table 1, p.7.
  - Note: auto exploration is 22.3 points below the oracle and demos are 11.2 points below. The authors still call them "comparable".
    - quote: "Their results consistently outperformed the GPT-4 baseline and are comparable to the results of human-written documents"
    - where: p.7.

- The authors attribute the action-space gain to coordinate prediction being hard for the LLM.
  - number: none
  - quote: "Our observations indicate that LLM struggles with producing accurate xy coordinates, while our simplified action space eliminates this challenging requirement."
  - where: p.7.
  - This ties to the note's coordinate-prediction material.

- In a Lightroom image-editing user study, documented agents ranked better than the baseline.
  - number: average rank (lower is better) 2.30 baseline, 1.95 watching demos, 1.75 manual. Tools used 2.4, 5.8 and 4.0.
  - setup: 5 images with visual issues such as low contrast and overexposure. The task was "fix this image until it looks good to you". A user study ranked the outputs. The paper does not say how many raters took part or how the ranking was collected.
  - quote: "GPT4 (Baseline) NoneOurs2.30 2.4 AppAgent Watching Demos Ours1.95 5.8Manually Crafted Ours1.75 4.0"
  - where: Table 2, p.7. Discussion on pp.7-8.
  - The baseline row is jumbled in the extraction. The text says documented agents use more tools: "with a document, the agent tends to use various tools to improve the image quality, while the GPT-4 baseline uses fewer tools."

- The framework design is a two-phase loop that needs no model training.
  - number: none
  - quote: "eliminating the need to adapt the parameters of the LLMs or collect extensive training data for each app."
  - where: p.2.

SETUP DETAILS
- The benchmark has 10 apps: "Google Maps, Twitter, Telegram, YouTube, Spotify, Yelp, Gmail, TEMU, Clock, and Lightroom". The abstract and Fig.1 say "50 tasks across 10 different Apps". Table 1 reports "the average performance of 45 tasks on 9 of the 10 previously described apps". Lightroom is excluded "as assessing task completion in this application presented inherent ambiguities", so the headline 50 and 10 differ from the scored 45 and 9.
- The model is GPT-4 (the paper also says GPT-4V in related work). It is one model with no model comparison.
- Step caps: "For the exploration phase, we capped the maximum number of steps at 40. During testing, we limited the maximum number of steps to 10."
- Success rate: "If the agent fails to finish the task in 10 steps, it is considered a failure."
- Reward: a hand-scored model where "closer the UI page was to the objective, the higher the score". It gives partial credit from the final state. No scale is given. The values run up to 5.5, so it is not 0-1.
- Average steps: counted over successfully finished tasks only. Compare steps across rows with care, since the rows have different success sets.
- Number of runs, variance and confidence intervals: not reported.
- Observation inputs: a screenshot plus an XML file of interactive elements. Each element gets a numeric ID overlaid on the screenshot. The ID comes from the resource ID, or from class name, size and content.
- Action space: Tap, Long_press (1 s), Swipe(element, direction, short/medium/long), Text, Back, Exit. This is six actions (the paper says "four basic functions" and then lists six).
- Exploration modes:
  - Autonomous: trial and error, comparing before and after screenshots. It writes a per-element document and updates it on repeat visits. It backs out of irrelevant pages such as ads. It is described as goal-oriented, "Compared with random exploration, such as Depth-First Search and Breadth-First Search". It stops when the assigned task is complete.
  - Watching demos: a human operates the app and the agent records "only the elements and actions employed by the human". The paper calls this "often more effective" yet gives only 84.4% against 73.3%. No tasks, demo counts or exploration cost are given.
- Deployment loop per step: observe, think, act, then summarise history. The summary is carried into the next prompt as memory.

LIMITS
- The authors concede one limitation: the simplified action space means "advanced controls such as multi-touch and irregular gestures are not supported."
- Evaluation is small and single-model. It uses 45 scored tasks, no repeats, and a hand-built benchmark. The task list and the document-quality criteria are not given.
- The 95.6% oracle document and the demo documents are authored by the same team, and the baselines are not independent. There is no comparison with other GUI agents or other models. The only baseline is GPT-4 with and without a document, and with the raw or simplified action space.
- The paper reports no failure analysis, no cost or latency figures, no exploration cost, and no security or irreversible-action discussion, even though it claims "enhances security and privacy".
- The Lightroom study is subjective. The rater count is unstated and there are only 5 images.
- The paper claims generalization to unseen apps, but the apps are popular ones whose UIs GPT-4 may already know. It does not test this.
- It has dated. It relies on the Android XML accessibility tree, so it is not a pure-screenshot approach. Later work (CogAgent, UI-TARS, OSWorld-era agents, per the note) uses screenshots only and reports much harder benchmarks.

BUILDS ON
- Yao et al. 2023 (ReAct), cited for "synergizes reasoning and acting", with the observe-think-act loop.
- Yan et al. 2023 (GPT-4V in Wonderland) and Yang et al. 2023c (Dawn of LMMs), showing GPT-4V understands simple smartphone UIs.
- AutoGPT (Yang et al., 2023a), MetaGPT (Hong et al., 2023) and HuggingGPT (Shen et al., 2023) for the LLM-agent context.
- RT-2 (Brohan et al., 2023) and other embodied-agent work, as multimodal-agent context only.
- It does not cite earlier mobile UI-automation agents in a method role.

CODE: none. The only code-like items are the action signatures, such as `Swipe(element:int, direction:str, dist:str)` (p.4) and example calls such as `tap(5)` and `swipe(21,"up","medium")`.

FIGURES
- Fig. 1 (p.1): examples of tasks across apps with Observation, Thought and Action traces. It shows the output format.
- Fig. 2 (p.4): overview of the two phases, exploration producing a document and deployment consuming it. This is the quickest picture of the method.
- Fig. 3 (p.6): worked traces on Google Maps, Gmail and Lightroom, showing the per-step observation, thought and action. I did not run the figure script. The captions above are as printed in the text.

PROBLEMS
- The Table 1 and Table 2 extraction is jumbled. Row and column pairing is inferred from layout and from the arrow notes (SR↑, Reward↑, Avg. Steps), and the quotes above are copied as extracted.
- The arXiv stamp "5 Jul 2026" on a Dec 2023 paper looks like a revised version, so check it before citing a date.
- The text lists "four basic functions" and then six actions.
- No embedded instructions were found in the PDF.
- The target note's row says "50 tasks across 10 apps", but quantitative results cover only 45 tasks on 9 apps. This is worth correcting or qualifying. The note's description "knowledge base by exploring or watching a demonstration" matches the paper. Add the success rates 48.9%, 73.3%, 84.4% and 95.6% with their setup if it wants numbers.
